messages.author: 8d1674b7b16af1b1
messages.subject: imputation in finite mixture models
parts:
Hi all, hope you're having a nice weekend.

I'm having trouble with a finite mixture model that has censored observations, and I was hoping that you could help me figure out where I'm going wrong.

In the simplified version I've attached, we have a mixture of two fairly well-separated Gaussians, and the values above 1.0 are censored.  I'm trying to fit the model by imputation rather than integrating out the censored values because I've been having numerical problems with extreme outliers and the lccdf functions. 

I'm using one set of imputed values for each mixture component. I know how to do this kind of imputation with a hand-written Gibbs sampler or EM procedure, but I'm having trouble writing down the full/joint posterior distribution in a way that lets me integrate out the mixture components so that I can fit it in Stan (rather than just following an algorithm based on conditional distributions). 

Right now, for every data point (fully-observed or imputed), I just use `log_mix` on its prior association with each component and on the two component likelihoods. This seems to be the wrong thing to do, however.

1) Although the two Gaussians are pretty well-separated in the data, Stan's output says that both components have similar means and sd's.

2) The imputed values don't seem to be sufficiently constrained by the likelihood.  If the distribution used for imputing these values has a mean of -.2 and an sd of 1.2, we shouldn't be seeing any values near 14. So I'm clearly not sampling from the correct distribution for the imputed values (i.e. from truncated Gaussians with means and standard deviations specified by `mu[k]` and `sigma[k]`).

I think these issues have to do with "Priors and Effective Data Size in Mixture Models" (section 10.7 in version 2.12.1 of the manual). In particular, the second problem listed above seems like it could be explained if the likelihood's influence is being diluted across the two distributions. 

Is this something I could address by augmenting the likelihood for each component in proportion to (1-responsibility)? I'm concerned that anything I do to fix the conditional distributions for the imputed values will end up indirectly affecting the mixing proportions and break the rest of the model.

Thanks in advance for your thoughts on this.  Sorry if I'm missing something obvious. I didn't see anything in the manual about imputation specifically in the context of finite mixture models, and most of the papers I've found online are about Gibbs sampling or EM. As I said above, I haven't been able to translate those papers to a Stan-friendly with joint distributions rather than conditionals.

Dave


------------

data {
  int N_y;
  int N_cens;
  vector[N_y] y;

  // prior probability that points belong to component 1
  vector[N_y + N_cens] prior_prob;

  // The largest possible non-censored value for y
  real max_observable;
}
parameters {
  ordered[2] mu; // avoid label-switching
  real<lower=0> sigma[2];

  // One value for each censored point from each mixture component
  matrix<lower=max_observable>[N_cens, 2] imputed;
}
model {
  // Priors
  mu ~ normal(0, 1);
  sigma ~ normal(0, 1);
  for(i in 1:N_cens){
    for(j in 1:2){
      imputed[i,j] ~ normal(0, 3);
    }
  }

  for (i in 1:(N_y + N_cens)) {
    real log_lik[2];
    for (k in 1:2) {
      real Y;
      if (i <= N_y) {
        # Pull Y from the fully-observed vector, y
        Y = y[i];
      } else {
        # Pull Y from imputed's column k
        Y = imputed[i - N_y, k];
      }
      log_lik[k] = normal_lpdf(Y | mu[k], sigma[k]);
    }
    target += log_mix(prior_prob[i], log_lik[1], log_lik[2]);
  }
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] imputation in finite mixture models
parts:
Hi Andrew, thanks for the quick reply.  I don't think the problem is sigma hitting zero; as I said, the sigma values are around 1.2.

I've attached a set of graphs that should help clarify the problem.

The first graph shows the data-generating process.  Everything to the left of the vertical line is fully-observed, while data points to the right of the line are imputed.

The second graph shows the posterior predictive distribution. It doesn't correctly reconstruct the data-generating process because the two components overlap too much.

The third figure shows that the imputed values don't come from the correct distribution.  There are far too many samples greater than 5, compared to what one would expect if one sampled from the Gaussians in the second panel and discarded everything below the vertical line.

This is why I think the model I sent is sampling from the wrong distribution for the censored values (probably because they only get 50% of the constraints that they should from the likelihood function, on average).

Hope this helps clarify the problem.

Thanks,

Dave

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] imputation in finite mixture models
parts:
If you can implement the E part of EM, the restis
just the likelihood, and you can just plug that straight
into Stan as written along with priors.

In your code, I think the problem is here:

You're imputing two values for each missing Y, one for
each mixture component. You only want to impute a single
value for each one.

I didn't understand how you had the mixture responsibilities
in the form of prior probabilities.

You can vectorize the "imputed" variable (I think it's easier
to understand models when you use standard names for variables
in the model rather than "imputed"; or mix with "y_imp" or
something).

I'd rewrite this:

real log_lik[2];
for (k in 1:2) {
real Y;
if (i <= N_y) {
# Pull Y from the fully-observed vector, y
Y = y[i];
} else {
# Pull Y from imputed's column k
Y = imputed[i - N_y, k];
}
log_lik[k] = normal_lpdf(Y | mu[k], sigma[k]);
}
target += log_mix(prior_prob[i], log_lik[1], log_lik[2]);

using a function:

real normal_mix_lpdf(real y, real theta, vector mu, vector sigma) {
return log_mix(theta, normal_lpdf(y, mu[1], sigma[1]),
normal_lpdf(y, mu[2], sigma[2]));
}

and two loops (with "imputed" renamed "y_imputed" and
"prior_prob" renamed "lambda"):

for (n in 1:N_y)
y[n] ~ normal_mix(lambda[n], mu, sigma);

for (n in 1:N_cens)
y_imputed[n] ~ normal_mix(lambda[n], mu, sigma);

Or you could even put the loop inside log_mix and then just
have y ~ and y_imputed ~ in the body.

- Bob
